method: A Yagi-Uda is a driven element with a reflector behind it and any number of directors in front, all cut close to a half wavelength and spaced along a boom. The free-space wavelength is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in MHz. Three conventional starting families are offered, each a set of length and spacing ratios applied to that wavelength: compact (reflector 0.500, driven 0.478, first director 0.445, director taper 0.0012 per element, reflector spacing 0.10, director spacing 0.12), standard (0.495, 0.473, 0.440, 0.0015, 0.15, 0.20) and long (0.500, 0.470, 0.442, 0.0015, 0.20, 0.30). The reflector sits at 0 on the boom, the driven element one reflector spacing behind the first director, and each director a further director spacing along it, so the boom length is the reflector spacing plus the director spacing multiplied by the director count; the boom length is also reported in wavelengths because that is the figure comparable with published gain tables. Every director is shortened by the taper relative to the one before it, which keeps the lengths strictly decreasing down the boom. Frequencies are 10 to 3000 MHz, director counts are whole numbers from 0 to 20, and the three boom profiles are the only choices; blank, non-numeric, negative, out-of-range and fractional values and an unknown profile are refused with the field named rather than defaulted. Element diameter, insulated mountings, the balun, boom and mast interaction, element droop, mutual coupling and ground effects are not modelled, and no gain, front-to-back ratio or SWR is predicted: these are thin-element starting dimensions to cut slightly long and trim with an analyser. The page runs entirely in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.

sources.title: A Yagi-Uda array is a driven dipole with a slightly longer reflector behind it and progressively shorter directors in front, spaced along a boom, and its dimensions scale with the free-space wavelength.
Practical Yagi designs are described by a boom length in wavelengths together with element length and spacing ratios; longer booms with more directors carry the higher gain.

Director lengths taper shorter toward the front of the array, and element diameter, mounting hardware and nearby conductors shift the resonant length, so published dimensions are starting points that need trimming.
The free-space wavelength in metres is 299.792458 divided by the frequency in megahertz.
